passage: For two years I built my life around not panicking. I took the stairs to the ninth floor so I wouldn't be trapped in the lift. I sat by the door in every meeting. I said no to the office trip to Goa and invented a family function. I told nobody. It felt shameful, like a weakness I had to hide, even though I'm Zubin, the one who fixes everyone's laptops. Last winter Sangeeta, who shares my desk pod, found me pale on the stairwell. I finally told her everything. She didn't laugh. She said, "That sounds exhausting. Have you seen anyone about it?" That question got me to a psychologist. Months of practice later, I still get the odd wave, but I take the lift most days now. Telling one person made it lighter to carry.

qa.q: Which floor did Zubin climb the stairs to?
qa.a: Zubin took the stairs to the ninth floor.

qa.q: How did Zubin feel about the panic before telling anyone?
qa.a: Zubin felt ashamed and secretive, treating it as a weakness to hide, even inventing a family function.

qa.q: What turned things around for Zubin?
qa.a: Telling Sangeeta, and her question about seeing someone, which led Zubin to a psychologist and months of practice.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta have seen Zubin on the stairwell?
qa.a: Sangeeta seemed concerned rather than judging, calling it exhausting and gently asking if Zubin had seen anyone.

grounding: A working adult plans life around avoiding panic and hides it in shame, and telling one person and getting professional help ease it.

passage:
Supervisor's notebook, private. Indu Ramaswamy, warehouse B.
Asif has asked to swap out of the cold-storage shift four times this month. He gets sharp when pressed about it and eats lunch alone in his car. I assumed he disliked the work. Today he came to me, stared at the floor and said he gets panic attacks in the cold room, with its heavy door, and has hidden it for over a year because he thought I'd think less of him. He looked ashamed.
I thanked him for telling me and promised it stays between us. I've moved him to the packing line for now. I gave him the number for our employee counselling service and said many people recover well with proper help. He seemed lighter walking out. I'll check in with him quietly next Friday.

qa.q: How many times has Asif asked to swap out of the cold-storage shift this month?
qa.a: Four times this month.

qa.q: What was Asif feeling when he finally told Indu?
qa.a: Asif felt ashamed and afraid of being thought less of; he stared at the floor, but seemed lighter afterwards.

qa.q: Which of Indu's responses would help Asif most?
qa.a: Keeping it private, moving him to the packing line for now, sharing the counselling service number and planning a quiet check-in.

qa.q: How did Indu's view of Asif's swap requests change?
qa.a: Indu first assumed Asif disliked the work, but now sees the requests as a way of avoiding panic he had been hiding.

grounding: A working adult avoids a trigger and hides recurring panic out of shame, and telling one trusted person opens a path to professional help.

passage: For almost two years, I planned my life around the next attack. I took the stairs to the seventh floor and said it was for fitness. I sat nearest the door in every meeting. I skipped my team's offsite with a fake fever and turned down the Bengaluru transfer I'd wanted since college. Nobody knew. I'm Sunaina, and I was good at hiding. What I felt most wasn't fear, it was shame, as if needing an escape route made me weak. Then one night my flatmate Sangeeta found me on the bathroom floor, breathing hard, and I couldn't make up a story fast enough. So I told her everything. She didn't laugh. She made tea and sat with me, and the next week she helped me find a psychologist. Months later, I took the lift for the first time. Telling one person was the start.

qa.q: Which floor did Sunaina take the stairs to?
qa.a: The seventh floor.

qa.q: What did Sunaina feel most during those two years?
qa.a: Sunaina felt ashamed, as if needing an escape route made Sunaina weak.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Sunaina's recovery?
qa.a: Telling Sangeeta everything, and then getting help from a psychologist.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta have felt finding Sunaina on the bathroom floor?
qa.a: Sangeeta was probably shocked and worried, and chose to respond with calm care.

grounding: Shows a working adult who shapes life around avoiding panic, hiding it out of shame, and whose recovery begins by telling one person and getting professional help.

passage:
Team lead's note to self, March
Over the last few months I noticed that Ayesha always took the stairs, even with a heavy laptop bag, and slipped out of our crowded Monday meetings after ten minutes. She made excuses for the client dinner twice. I had started wondering if she was losing interest. Last week I asked her, privately and without any pressure, whether something was making work harder. After a long pause, she told me she has had panic attacks for a year, felt ashamed, and had been hiding them from everyone. I thanked her for trusting me. We agreed she could sit near the door and take short breaks without explaining. I also shared the details of the company's counselling service. Today she told me she has started seeing a therapist. I have kept this between us.
Jahnavi

qa.q: Which meetings did Ayesha slip out of?
qa.a: The crowded Monday meetings.

qa.q: How had Ayesha been feeling about the panic attacks?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and had been hiding them from everyone for a year.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi do that helped?
qa.a: Jahnavi asked privately without pressure, thanked Ayesha for trusting, agreed small changes and shared the counselling service.

qa.q: How might Ayesha experience telling one person at work?
qa.a: She may feel relieved and lighter, no longer carrying the secret alone, and more able to seek help.

grounding: Shows a working adult hiding recurring panic out of shame and planning around triggers, and how telling one trusted person and getting professional help eases the load.

passage:
Saturday night
I rode the metro today. Two stops, with Manjula next to me. First time in a year. Writing it down so it's real.
For a year I have booked autos I couldn't really afford the time for, left the house an hour early, and told everyone I 'just prefer the road'. Nobody knew about the episodes except Manjula, and I only told her last month because she caught me shaking at the station entrance. I'd felt so ashamed.
The psychologist gave me a plan: small steps, breathe out slow, let the sensations rise and fall. Today my heart did its thing at the first stop. I held the rail, breathed, and waited. It came down. Manjula squeezed my arm and didn't make a fuss.
Next week: four stops. It's strange how much lighter I feel with one person knowing.
Kavitha

qa.q: How many stops did Kavitha ride today?
qa.a: Two stops.

qa.q: How did Kavitha feel before telling Manjula?
qa.a: Kavitha felt ashamed and alone, hiding the episodes from everyone.

qa.q: What made today's ride possible?
qa.a: The psychologist's plan of small steps and slow breathing, plus Manjula's calm company.

qa.q: How might Manjula have felt on the metro beside Kavitha?
qa.a: Manjula was probably a little nervous but proud, choosing to stay calm and not make a fuss.

grounding: Shows a working adult who planned life around avoiding panic and hid it in shame, now recovering with professional guidance and one trusted person.

passage:
Abhinav: You bailed on the team offsite again. Everything ok?
Nikita: Honestly? No. Can I tell you something and you won't make it weird
Abhinav: Of course
Nikita: I've been having panic attacks. For months. Metro, meetings, the lift. I plan my whole day around avoiding them.
Nikita: I've told no one. It feels so embarrassing
Abhinav: Thank you for telling me. That sounds exhausting, not embarrassing
Nikita: I thought you'd think I'm weak
Abhinav: I think you're carrying a lot alone. Have you talked to a doctor or a therapist?
Nikita: No. Didn't think it could get better
Abhinav: My cousin went through this. With proper help she got a lot better. Want me to help you find someone?
Nikita: Ok. Yes. I already feel lighter just typing this 🤍

qa.q: Where has Nikita been having panic attacks?
qa.a: Metro, meetings, the lift.

qa.q: How did Nikita feel about keeping the panic secret?
qa.a: Nikita felt ashamed and embarrassed, afraid of seeming weak.

qa.q: What next step did Abhinav offer?
qa.a: To help find a doctor or therapist, since proper help often leads to recovery.

qa.q: How might Abhinav have felt reading Nikita's messages?
qa.a: Abhinav likely felt concerned and caring, and grateful to be trusted.

grounding: A working adult who plans life around avoiding panic feels ashamed, and telling one trusted person opens the way to professional help.
